name: GraphQL-core
vendor: GraphQL-Python community (created and maintained by Christoph Zwerschke)
summary: The Python port of GraphQL.js: the parser, validator and executor that Strawberry, Ariadne and Graphene all run on.
intro: GraphQL-core is a Python port of GraphQL.js, the reference implementation of GraphQL, and it copies that code as closely as Python allows, down to a test suite of more than 3,000 unit tests that mirrors the JavaScript one. It does two things: it builds a type schema, and it runs requests against that schema. You build a schema from objects such as `GraphQLObjectType` and `GraphQLField`, and give fields a `resolve` function. A resolver gets the parent value and a `GraphQLResolveInfo` object, whose `context` holds per-request state such as the logged-in user or a database session. Field arguments arrive as keyword arguments, where GraphQL.js passes them as one object. `graphql_sync()` parses the document, validates it against the schema and only then executes it. `graphql()` does the same for resolvers that are coroutines, using `asyncio`. There’s no HTTP layer, so most people never call it directly: Graphene, Ariadne and Strawberry build their schemas with it and run every query through its executor.

The version numbers follow GraphQL.js, not SemVer: a new major version of GraphQL.js becomes a new minor version of GraphQL-core, and that minor version can break the API. Version 3.3.0 (September 27, 2026) follows GraphQL.js 17.0.2 and supports Python 3.10 to 3.15. It adds incremental delivery with `@defer` and `@stream` (experimental, following the current spec proposal), cancellation with an `AbortSignal`, and immutable AST nodes. The 3.2 line (3.2.13) still follows GraphQL.js 16 for projects that need Python 3.7 to 3.9. The maintainers recommend pinning with `~= 3.3.0`.
strengths: Tracks the reference implementation closely and ports its tests, so parsing, validation and execution behave like GraphQL.js
One engine under the main Python libraries: Strawberry, Ariadne and Graphene all build on it, so spec fixes reach all of them
Type hints throughout, checked with mypy, and resolvers can be plain functions or `asyncio` coroutines
Keeps up with the spec: 3.3 brings GraphQL.js 17 features such as `@defer` and `@stream` to Python
limits: Low level: schemas are built from verbose `GraphQLField` and `GraphQLArgument` objects, and there’s no server, so applications usually use a library on top
Not SemVer: a minor release can break the API, so dependents pin a patch range such as `~= 3.3.0`
Asynchronous execution only through `asyncio`; GraphQL-core 2’s other executors are gone
Incremental delivery (`@defer`, `@stream`) and fragment arguments are experimental and follow spec proposals that may still change

story: Facebook published GraphQL.js in July 2015, and Python got its own port within months. Syrus Akbary released the first `graphql-core` package in October 2015: a port of GraphQL.js that also ran on Python 2.7, and the engine under Graphene, which Akbary also created. That port, now called GraphQL-core 2, stayed at the level of GraphQL.js 0.6.0.

In 2018 Christoph Zwerschke released GraphQL-core-next, a re-implementation for modern Python 3 that followed the then-current GraphQL.js 14 closely, added type hints and replicated its test suite. Its first public release, 1.0.0, came out in September 2018. Ariadne moved onto it in January 2019 because it supported `async` resolvers and a newer version of the spec. In November 2019 it was released as GraphQL-core 3.0.0, the successor to both GraphQL-core 2 and GraphQL-core-next.

Since then each GraphQL.js major version has become a GraphQL-core minor version: 3.1 followed GraphQL.js 15 in April 2020, 3.2 followed GraphQL.js 16 in January 2022, and 3.3 followed GraphQL.js 17 in September 2026, after a long run of alpha releases from 2022 on. Graphene 3, Ariadne and Strawberry all build on it.

choices.choice: Port the reference implementation, tests included
choices.why: The goal was to stay very close to GraphQL.js while offering a Pythonic API. Replicating its whole test suite with pytest keeps behavior compatible and makes each new GraphQL.js release straightforward to port.

choices.choice: Minor versions follow GraphQL.js major versions
choices.why: A breaking release of GraphQL.js usually forces breaking changes in the port. Mapping it to a minor version keeps the major version at 3, and only patch releases promise full backward compatibility.
GraphQL.js was typed with Flow and later TypeScript. The port uses Python type hints the same way, checked with mypy, which also helps the libraries built on top of it.

choices.choice: Drop legacy Python and custom executors
choices.why: GraphQL-core 2 supported old Python versions and several executors. The rewrite aimed to be simple and cruft-free for current Python, so it supports asynchronous execution only through `asyncio`.

timeline.text: First `graphql-core` release by Syrus Akbary, in October
GraphQL-core-next 1.0.0, based on GraphQL.js 14, in September
GraphQL-core 3.0.0 replaces GraphQL-core 2 and GraphQL-core-next in November
